notedTerms.reasoning: Confirmed: no Spanish source writes this as one word. Alpine's Spanish tutorial says 'para hacer que el evento sólo se dispare una vez'; the Spanish Vue docs say 'se activará como máximo una vez'; lenguajejs describes addEventListener's once option as 'Sólo ejecuta la función una primera vez'. Since the runtime collapses hyphens to a space before matching, 'una-vez' is shippable; there is no single Spanish word for 'once (one time)' and inventing one would repeat the defect.

familyTokens.reasoning: DEFECT. 'Morfar' is not a Spanish technical word — it is Río de la Plata lunfardo meaning 'to eat', established enough to have its own Wiktionary entry, so an Argentine/Uruguayan/Paraguayan developer reads fx-intercambio="morfar" and window.morfar() as 'eat'. Spanish 3D/graphics literature keeps morph/morphing untranslated. 'transformar' is the dictionary rendering; 'fusionar' is defensible since idiomorph self-describes as a DOM-merging algorithm.

DEFECT, exactly as suspected. In Spanish 'cabecera' is the standard word for an HTTP *header*, not the HEAD method — every Spanish explanation of HEAD uses it that way ('solo solicita las cabeceras del servidor'). So cabecera() reads as 'header'. NOTE: this is a rexi global (window.cabecera), so a hyphenated multi-word form is NOT available — it must be a valid JS identifier. Spanish docs universally keep HTTP method names in English.

No Spanish source glosses POST as 'publicar' — a literal calque of English 'post' in its blog sense. MDN es: POST 'se utiliza para enviar una entidad a un recurso'. 'crear' is a defensible alternative.

'Poner' is a word-for-word calque carrying none of the method's meaning. MDN es ('reemplaza todas las representaciones actuales') and the Spanish REST tutorial ('PUT: reemplazar') converge, and it gives beginners the PUT-vs-PATCH contrast for free.
Well attested: 'obtener información' / 'recuperar datos de un servidor'.
The Spanish REST tutorial's summary line is literally 'DELETE: eliminar'.
Real Spanish verb used in the software sense, weakly but genuinely attested. No better single token.

False-friend calque — Spanish uses 'prevenir' for forestalling illness or risk. Spanish JS writing about preventDefault reaches for 'evitar' or 'cancelar' ('evitar que se ejecuten'; MDN es 'Cancela el evento').
'Detener la propagación' is the fixed Spanish collocation. Correct — but see `halt`: shipping detener and parar side by side is the real problem.

Not a fused compound but worse for a learner: 'parar' and 'detener' are near-perfect synonyms in Spanish (every synonym dictionary lists each as the primary gloss of the other), so an author cannot remember which of .parar/.detener is halt and which is stop. 'abortar' is an established Spanish computing verb, unambiguously distinct. Low evidence — no Spanish source discusses a 'halt' modifier since it is moxi-specific.
See notedTerms.

Spanish renders .self as 'el propio elemento' or 'el elemento de sí mismo' — never a bare 'mismo', which standing alone is a dangling adjective meaning 'same'. 'propio' carries the self sense unaided; 'si-mismo' is now available given hyphen folding.
'Clic fuera de un elemento' is exactly how Spanish tutorials title this pattern.
'Fase de captura' is standard. Noun form correct — it names a phase, not an action.
'Eventos pasivos' is established; lenguajejs uses it as a section heading.

Literal calque; in Spanish 'en vivo' belongs to broadcasting, not data binding. The Spanish word for what moxi's `live` marks — an element whose bindings update automatically — is 'reactivo' ('datos reactivos', 'reactividad'), the term every Spanish Vue/Svelte tutorial uses.

The best token in the whole Spanish set: `al` + noun/infinitive is precisely the Spanish construction for English 'on X-ing'. 'al hacer clic' / 'al enviar el formulario' are the exact phrases Spanish tutorials use. `al-clic` reads as natural Spanish rather than a translation.
Correctly an infinitive — this is a directive to the library, not an event name, so the imperative reading is intended, as in the English original.

Imperative-reading and inconsistent with its siblings: 'abrir' is 'open it!', but the SSE open event reports that the connection was established. Spanish SSE writing says 'la conexión está abierta'. The participle matches `intercambiado`, already a participle.
Same defect: es.javascript.info uses 'Cierra la conexión' for the close() *method*, whereas the event announces it already closed. 'cerrado' disambiguates event from method.
Exact and universal.
Correctly a past participle, the right shape for an event reporting a completed action. Consistent with fx-intercambio.

attrs.reasoning: Spanish HTML pedagogy glosses <form action> directly as 'la acción'. Transparent cognate, no rival.
MDN es defines the attribute verbatim as 'El método HTTP que el navegador usa'.

'Disparar un evento' is near-universal across Spain and Latin America, so 'disparador' is the natural agent noun. Competitors are domain-bound: 'desencadenador' is Microsoft SQL localization, 'activador' is Google Tag Manager UI, 'gatillo' is a firearm calque.
'Elemento objetivo' is established; MDN es glosses it as 'el target (objetivo) actual del evento'. Weakest keep of the five — 'destino' is a real competitor — but not weak enough to churn.
Spanish htmx writeups reach for intercambiar unprompted. Semantically safer than 'reemplazo', which would mislead about beforeend/afterbegin; 'cambio' is taken by the change event.

events.reasoning: RAE-sanctioned noun, universal across Spain and Latin America; only the surrounding verb varies (hacer clic / clicar / cliquear / pulsar), which loka does not ship.
Noun form, correct event reading. 'cambiar' is the imperative-reading form and should stay second.
Exactly right. Caveat: the third synonym 'someter' is an English-influenced calque Spanish style authorities do not endorse for form submission — harmless in last position but should not be taught.
Weakly attested — Spanish sources describe the event functionally rather than naming it — but 'entrada' is the standard noun and has no rival.

IMPERATIVE. 'enfocar' is 'focus it!' and is also the Spanish name of the elem.focus() *method*, so it collides with the action rather than naming the event. es.javascript.info titles its chapter 'Enfocado: enfoque/desenfoque' — the noun pair is the established event naming. Swap primary and alternate.

Spanish does NOT have the de/ja/ko image-blur defect: 'desenfoque' is built on 'foco', same root as 'enfoque', and es.javascript.info uses 'enfoque/desenfoque' as the Spanish names of the focus/blur pair. Only the word class needs fixing — promote the noun over the infinitive. 'perder-foco' would be an intelligible extra synonym.
IMPERATIVE — 'iniciar' is 'start it!'. No direct Spanish source since init is a fixi coinage, so this is a consistency judgement, not an evidence finding.

CALQUE. In Spanish 'abajo' is purely spatial ('key below') and does not carry the pressed sense English 'down' has in this compound. Sources are unanimous: 'el evento keydown se activa cuando se presiona cualquier tecla'; aprenderaprogramar's whole lesson is titled 'Tecla pulsada'. 'tecla-presionada' is the equally good LatAm-leaning variant.
Same calque — 'arriba' reads as 'above', not 'released'. Sources: 'el keyup se produce al soltar una tecla presionada'.

DISAGREES WITH THE 2026-05-23 SETTLED DECISION, as the brief invites. Un-fusing 'ratónabajo' fixed the orthography but left the underlying calque: 'ratón abajo' means 'mouse below' and does not say a button was pressed. Spanish sources describe mousedown as 'se pulsa un botón del ratón'. 'ratón-pulsado' preserves parallelism with the keydown fix and means the right thing.
Same disagreement — 'arriba' is spatial and loses the release sense.
Correct and idiomatic, unlike the abajo/arriba pair — Spanish genuinely uses the spatial preposition here: 'cuando el cursor del ratón se encuentra por encima de una determinada zona'.
Intelligible and spatially correct. 'ratón-sale' would be closer to source verbs but 'fuera' pairs cleanly with 'encima'.
IMPERATIVE — 'desplazar' is 'move it!'. 'Desplazamiento' is the established noun ('barra de desplazamiento', which every Spanish speaker knows). Clearest infinitive-to-noun swap in the set.

IMPERATIVE FLAG but keep: Spanish has no usable noun ('redimensión' is rare; sources go descriptive). If the noun-primary convention is adopted set-wide, 'cambio-de-tamaño' is now available given hyphen folding.
Correctly a noun and correctly the Spanish term. Keep 'cargar' as second-position alternate only.

variantSplit.reasoning: No split warranted. Only one candidate has substance — ratón vs mouse — and the boundary does not hold in the developer register: RAE's Diccionario panhispánico de dudas documents 'ratón' as practically exclusive in Spain and 'mouse' as predominant in América at the general-vocabulary level, but Platzi (Colombia) writes 'el ratón' throughout its mouse-events article while es.javascript.info and Argentine tutorials write 'mouse'. That is a per-author preference crossing the region line, not a region boundary. Following the pt and zh conclusions in this wave, the fix is extra synonyms in the same es map: add 'mouse-pulsado' / 'mouse-soltado' / 'mouse encima' / 'mouse fuera' alongside the ratón forms, primary-first keeping ratón as taught. Everything else is invariant. One near-miss: 'morfar' is a Río de la Plata problem, not a Spain/LatAm token split — no rival token exists in Spain either, so it is a correctness fix rather than a split.

overall: Two defect classes dominate and cut across the whole Spanish set. First, DIRECTIONAL CALQUES: 'unavez' is malformed as suspected, but the same English-shaped thinking produced 'tecla abajo/arriba' and 'ratón abajo/arriba', where Spanish abajo/arriba is purely spatial and carries none of the pressed/released sense — so un-fusing 'ratónabajo' in May fixed the orthography while leaving the mistranslation; pulsado/soltado is the evidence-backed fix. Second, INFINITIVE-VS-NOUN: enfocar, desenfocar, desplazar, iniciar, abrir and cerrar all read as commands to the runtime rather than reports that something happened, and Spanish has ready nouns or participles for nearly all (enfoque, desenfoque, desplazamiento, inicio, abierto, cerrado); es.javascript.info's own chapter title 'Enfocado: enfoque/desenfoque' is the cleanest evidence. Spanish does NOT share the de/ja/ko blur defect. The two worst individual terms are both in the never-reviewed set: 'morfar' means 'to eat' in Río de la Plata lunfardo, and 'cabecera' is the Spanish word for an HTTP header so rexi's HEAD verb is named after the wrong thing. THREE THINGS THE BRIEF DID NOT ASK: (a) rexi and paxi globals become window[alias], so they must be valid JS identifiers — the hyphenated-multiword answer that works for moxi modifiers is NOT available for obtener/publicar/poner/cabecera/morfar; (b) moxi ships 'parar' for halt alongside 'detener' for stop, dictionary synonyms in Spanish, so the pair is unlearnable regardless of wording; (c) the moxi global 'transicion' ships without its accent while fx-acción and fx-método ship with theirs, and since lookup folds case and separators but NOT accents, a Spanish author who correctly types transición() gets a ReferenceError. Context for all of it: there is essentially no Spanish-language htmx corpus, so loka is coining this vocabulary rather than adopting it.
